items.content:
You're not a rocket scientist 🚀, so stop being surprised that your latest forecast shit the bed again.

We are hearing increasingly that with "quantum leaps" (marketer words, not mine) in technology - in ML, in particular - that huge gains are there for the taking for savvy forecasters. Some bold/delusional solutions salespeople go so far as to promise 20 or 30% improvements in your forecast.

The problem is, you're not doing rocket science. You're trying to predict the outcome of something so much more complex that the vast majority of practitioners and tools give up on causality before they start and resort to auto-regression.

With over a hundred trillion neural connections in each human brain, it makes a credible argument for being the most complex structure in the universe. Multiply that by many humans in any market, and you have a system whose innate variability is so high that you will not have anything better than directional success except in very specific, controlled applications.

The issue isn't that you need stronger math. 😂 It is true we have many multiples more computing power now than we did when we last landed people on the moon. But we were able to do so with little more than a slide rule because the first principles equations we used were based on a solid EMPIRICAL understanding of the entirety of the system. That is, all of the variables at play. 

The residuals in many physics experiments are so small BECAUSE THE SYSTEM IS SO WELL UNDERSTOOD that they can be used to accurately account for minute seismic movements across the Pacific when observing waves lapping on the beach in California.

In real life, many companies are lucky to see 40% error margins at a meaningful granularity and horizon not because they need better software. Or consultants. Not because humans made their math-based forecast worse (although that happens a lot). But because the nature of their value chain is based on millions of conscious and unconscious decisions being made in real-time by humans whose motivations and behaviours at an individual level remain predictably elusive.

There are too many unknown unknowns to delude oneself into the misapprehension that we are doing hard science. People selling solutions hate the sound of that but it's true. It is why very few practitioners look at causality and even fewer have success using it predictively. 

We are at the end of the day giving up on the "why" and looking at the "what" and, with varying degrees of success, predicting that what happened before will happen again.

What does that mean?

1️⃣ Begin by understanding based on your value chain what is possible from forecasting.

2️⃣ Understand what the cost/benefit of forecast improvement is in your specific context.

3️⃣ Be realistic about what you can achieve through forecasting, and focus effort where ROI is the greatest (Supplier performance management, BOM consolidation/simplification, lead time variability reduction initiatives, etc.)

items.content:
Landing at #YVR last night with my youngest son, we wanted to grab a quick drink before the car ride back home.

Lee's Donuts now has a location in Domestic Arrivals and at this time of evening, had the market cornered on a place to get a drink. They were also contending with their leftover inventory from the day and were offering donuts at 50% off. How many we bought is not the point of this post. 😆

The gentleman working there volunteered that his manager had overbought inventory that day based on expectations of increased volume from the FIFA World Cup kicking off in Vancouver (and cities across North America) last night.

And this, to me, underlines the fundamental limitation in the definition of "Demand Planning" as presented by people selling you software and quick Forecast Accuracy fixes.

Forecasting is not Demand Planning. At all. It isn't a plan, for starters.

Software isn't going to tell a new retail location selling donuts during a once in a generation event how many donuts to buy.

Extrapolating intrinsic demand patterns from history to (ultimately naively, though not always incorrectly) assume that the future will look like a version of it is something computers can do reasonably well. And humans don't typically add a lot of value here.

But that is not Demand Planning. That is time series forecasting. And it often counts for exactly zero in the real world.

Demand Planning is the work that Manager at Lee's Donuts did to use the information they had available and to derive a reasonable range of demand values for the day. Executing against that plan weighed the upside benefit of the high end against the downside cost of the low end and determined a plan that met their risk tolerance.

At ten minutes from closing I addressed 20% of their inventory issue at a price that was probably still profitable on a per unit basis, and two employees happily went home with the small balance of the inventory resulting from the demand call.

About three weeks ago I wrote a post teasing an update that would have meant a monumental change to NorthFind Management. A fairly expansive NDA stands in the way of telling a detailed story about this, but suffice it to say that one of the world's largest consultancies liked what they were seeing about our client value delivery and service, and spent the last five months selling the idea of using their expansive network and resources to allow us to do so at scale.

And, I will be honest: the idea of a Big 4 aggressively trying to acquire us with the explicit goal of having us change and improve their GTM in the Operations advisory space was good for the ego.

But as time went on and more and more stakeholders were pulled in for consultation and opinion, there were a few questions I was having more and more difficulty answering satisfactorily:

- Am I certain that post merger my team and I would be able to continue to deliver the kind of value and action focused client support that we have for the last 15 years?

- Am I certain that we would retain the flexibility to meet the unique requirements of all our clients at whatever point that are at in their Operations journey, and not try to have them conform to a single, scripted approach?

- Am I certain that we would not be offering advisory and managed services as an adjunct to software sales (whereas today we never sell software, and see it as a tool rather than a solution)?

NorthFind began in direct response to the rigid profit-driven (this is consultant, not client profit) approach to many consultants in the Operations Management space. We have consistently seen ourselves as partners who get into the weeds, get scarred, and help drag people across the finish line. Our primary motivation remain client success because we don't have shareholders or partners with quarterly income disbursement expectations to meet.

This morning, on what will be my final call with these consultants, it was clear to me I couldn't answer these questions appropriately. It was clear that the big news is that NorthFind has a model built on client outcomes, and there is no need to change it. And having dodged a bullet, I'm excited to return 100% of our focus to where it belongs: What can we do to help you do what you do better?

Adoption of FVA is now widespread enough that there are plenty of people who don't really know where it came from (thanks Michael Gilliland) and how best to make use of it.

As one of the earlier proponents of FVA, I used it in particular to highlight process steps that were yielding negative ROI. For me, forecasting has never been about considering Accuracy a performance indicator. It is a process diagnostic metric. Real business performance is measured in dollars.

Understanding how a forecast impacts the P&L is a lot more useful than blindly throwing all your eggs (and money) into the forecasting basket and assuming that ROI comes out the other end. Depending on the nature of your business, it often doesn't. This was a lesson I learned early on during my time in the tire industry. Portfolio complexity and limited shipment windows for seasonal tires meant deterministic forecasts, no matter how sophisticated the software, were not up to the challenge of inventory positioning on their own. 

ROI may better be achieved through lead-time optimization and control initiatives; through multi-echelon inventory optimization; or through more effective supplier performance management.

FVA used properly - join Crystal, John and I in Montreal to learn more - allows me to understand the limitations of forecasting and whether there are other areas in enterprise planning that will better lead to delighted customers and shareholders.

repost.content:
Your PivotTable already knows the % change.
Most people add a helper column anyway.

Right-click the value → Show Values As → % Difference From. 

That's it. 

The pivot calculates it, updates when you filter, recalculates when you refresh.

One detail that trips most people up:
When you set the base item to "Previous," that doesn't mean "previous month." 

It means the previous visible cell in the pivot. In a month-by-month layout it happens to be the same thing. 

Change the layout to quarters, and "Previous" now means previous quarter.

Same setting. Different meaning. 

Whatever the pivot shows, that's what "Previous" refers to.

If you build monthly reports, this one's worth knowing cold.

We just passed 3,000,000 subscribers on YouTube.
10 years ago, some of my corporate friends made fun of me for starting a YouTube channel. 

Fair enough. 
Corporate people didn't really take YouTube seriously back then.

But here's what 10 years and 3 million people taught me:

#1 - Don't box yourself in
I deliberately never named my channel "Excel." 
I knew I didn't want to be stuck in one lane. But even then, it took me years to actually post something outside of Excel because I was scared my audience wouldn't approve.

Then last year, I posted something completely different. 
A Rubik's cube tutorial. 
Yes. A Rubik's cube! On an Excel channel.

That video now has 3,000,000 views. It's actually still our #1 most watched video. Hundreds of people have commented that they finally solved a Rubik's cube because of it.

I almost didn't post it. I teach tools like Excel and Power BI. But I realized, my main thing is helping people solve problems. It doesn't always have to be Excel. 
After all, I left corporate because I didn't want to be boxed in. It didn't make sense to create that box in my own business.

#2 - Do things you're passionate about and stop overthinking it.
The Rubik's cube wasn't a strategy. I just loved it. 
Not everything has to be strategy. What's the fun in work if you can't take some time and do things you love.

#3 - Know when to switch from "growth mode" to "sustainable mode."
For years, I posted every week. Then twice a week. There was a time I posted three times. I was terrified that if I stopped, everything would collapse.

Then I started getting stressed out. I was working on videos, courses, everything. And I had a YouTuber friend whose burnout got so bad he couldn't turn the camera on anymore. Beautiful channel. But he just couldn't do it anymore.

I took a month off. I didn't want to start hating what I loved.
Nothing collapsed. The channel was fine.

Your stats do go down when you post less. But you have to decide what matters more. I love teaching, and I want to keep doing this for a while. So I found a pace I can actually sustain.

It's like losing weight. You need the calorie deficit to get there. But at some point, you have to eat in a way you can live with. And only you know when that point is.

I'm grateful for 3 million. But that's just a number. What makes me happier is reading the comments below the videos from people sharing their wins. Whether it's solving a Rubik's cube or getting a promotion because they finally learned Power Query.

What's something you almost didn't do but are really glad you did?

So this is what happened the last two weeks.

I was at the LinkedIn Learning studios in Carpinteria, California. Recording an Excel course. My first time there.
 
There were 3 people in the room with me the entire time: a director, a producer, and a video production tech. This wasn't just "hit record and talk." They were listening for clarity, transitions, pacing, energy.
 
Here’s something people don’t realize. I didn’t either when I first started recording: 

When you watch a polished video and think, “that was smooth”, you’re seeing the edit. The raw footage is usually full of pauses, retakes and stumbles.
 
Plus the camera dumps your energy just like it dumps your makeup. You have to bring WAY more energy than feels natural just to look normal on screen. The hardest part was switching between eye contact with the camera and screen recordings without losing my train of thought or letting the energy drop.
 
Before any recordings, weeks went into prepping the exercise files and scripting.
 
Now it's in the hands of the editors. From the early cuts I've seen so far, it looks great. 

I'll share more when I have a date. If you use #Excel even a little, you’ll want to keep an eye out for it.

Many thanks to the awesome and super fun production team!

Most of us wouldn't drop an Excel file in ChatGPT to analyze. We'd open Excel. Maybe get help from Copilot.
But it turns out that plenty of people can't be bothered to open Excel. They drag the file into ChatGPT and go with it.

So I was curious. Could it actually handle a proper file? 

Not a clean one-tab example. But multiple sheets it had to relate on its own, even where the column headers didn't match. Also no formulas. It would have to write the calculations on its own.

I lined up four questions, each harder than the last. I was sure it would fall apart on the third one. Here's what happened: https://lnkd.in/dYsa2Fjs

BTW - I think it's totally fine to use ChatGPT or any AI for ad-hoc analysis. For recurring reporting build a deterministic model with Power Query and Power Pivot instead.

items.content:
Just got back from Global Excel Summit in London.
BTW that cape on the table isn't mine. I usually don't take it to conferences. 

Victor Momoh tackled the thing most people are quietly avoiding, and walked through it step by step until it actually clicked. Yep. REGEX.

Ann K. Emery covered 40! visualization tips in 40 minutes. It was full of golden nuggets.

Damien Bird from Microsoft showed how Power Automate and Copilot Studio can work together. A smooth live demo right on stage. Which is harder than it looks.

Jakob Nielsen also from Microsoft showed us how we can build our own data types in Excel with the Data Types add-in. Since organization data types are retired from Excel, this is the best replacement.

Unpivot had an in person session on Power BI vs Excel. Real, funny, and honest about where each one actually wins.

And Mark Proctor proved Excel can play Taylor Swift songs. 🎸 
That wasn't his only point. He also showed how Excel handles values in the backend, and how sometimes 1<>1 in Excel. Standup comedy meets the advanced stuff we thought we already knew.

I had the honor of opening the event. Talking about the topics that are my top interests right now. Python's data science libraries and how complex time series analysis is actually realistically possible in Excel. Unlike what some articles might claim.

The thread running through almost every session: 
Excel isn't one tool anymore. It's a toolbox. And the toolbox keeps growing.

Ian Schnoor, put it well. Don't marry a single club. Every tool has strengths and weaknesses. The goal is finding the right fit for the situation and the person.

Danielle Stein Fairhurst and Cristiano Galvao both made the case that even as AI takes on more, the human in the chain still matters. And yes, we might get annoyed with AI for many reasons but how we interact and how we ask AI stuff, matters a lot.

Great to catch up with Oz du Soleil and many others I usually just see once a year. I met many members of our Python in Excel and Power Query courses. Thanks to everyone for stopping by and telling me a bit about your stories.

Huge thanks to Elena Lalovska, Tea Kuseva and the whole DATEL Productions Ltd. team for putting this together. And to Fay Bordbar and Giles Male for being such fun, easygoing hosts.
